strengths: Well-articulated problem motivation: clearly identifies the limitation of windowed self-attention (SCOT) in achieving global coupling and demonstrates how this leads to drift in closed-loop autoregressive rollouts.

Thoughtful architectural design with strong physical intuition: controlled low-frequency mixing respects separation of scales, bandwise radial gating avoids artifacts and width inflation, and additive fusion preserves feature dimensionality—all choices are well justified.

Comprehensive experimental validation: consistent improvements across 6 benchmarks (7-54% error reduction), proper matched training conditions, thorough ablation studies (Table 4), and insightful spectral analysis (Figure 4) demonstrating how components target different frequency bands.

Theoretical contributions: Lipschitz bounds (Appendix A) comparing DRIFT to Swin-style attention, formal proof that radial gating is energy non-expansive (Lemma A.3), and Sobolev-weighted defect bounds (Appendix B) provide rigor beyond empirical results.

Strong reproducibility: code available, detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1), comprehensive implementation details in appendices, and clear error-time analysis (Figures 2-3) directly addressing the drift motivation.
Modularity and efficiency: unit can replace windowed attention blocks in existing backbones, achieves 15% parameter reduction and higher throughput (158 vs 118 steps/s) than SCOT.
Excellent ablation design: removing each component (LFM, RG, FWL) produces measurable degradation; bandwise spectral error analysis (Figure 4) provides mechanistic insight into why components matter.
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to 2D Navier-Stokes (4 POSEIDON + 2 ApeBench variants). No evaluation on other PDE families (heat, Burgers, wave equations) or irregular domains despite mentioning these as future work. This limits claims about generality of the approach.

Non-automated spectral decomposition: low-frequency mask is hand-tuned initially; cutoff values κx, κy are learnable but task-specific. Section 6 acknowledges this and lists learning spectral partitions end-to-end as future work, but for a method emphasizing principled design, this is a meaningful limitation.

Insufficient analysis of computational cost on large grids: paper claims FFTs add 'memory traffic and latency on very large grids' (Section 6) but provides no empirical evidence. Throughput metrics use moderate resolution (H×W for grid size not explicitly stated). This concern is acknowledged but unsubstantiated.

Incremental novelty: dual spectral-spatial branches exist (UFNO mentioned), radial gating borrows from prior work (Rahaman et al. 2019, Xu et al. 2020), frequency-weighted loss from image processing (Fuoli et al. 2021). Innovation lies in careful *combination* rather than novel primitives. Missing comparisons to other recent hybrid methods (AFNO, U-NO, CNO not directly compared).

Modest improvement magnitudes: while consistent, gains are typically 10-20% (mean across tasks ~20%), with NS-PwC (53.6%) being an outlier. For a 30% acceptance venue, these incremental improvements, though reliable, may not meet the bar for significant impact.

Theoretical results lack direct connection to practice: Lipschitz bounds (Prop A.2) establish DRIFT has smaller worst-case gain than Swin but don't prove contractivity or guarantee error reduction. Sobolev bound (Theorem B.1) is interesting but relationship to actual PDE solution error is not established. Bounds feel supportive rather than predictive.

Insufficient hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: frequency-weighted loss has λ and α; paper states 'moderate values suffice' without ablation or sensitivity study. No guidance on setting these across different PDE types or parameter regimes.

Missing out-of-distribution and transfer evaluation: no zero-shot transfer tests (e.g., to different Reynolds numbers, initial condition distributions, or equation variants). Generalization beyond training distribution is important for foundation model claims but not demonstrated.

Presentation issues: spectral pipeline details (Section 4.2-4.3) are dense with notation; the ⊮ operator in Eq 4.1 usage is non-standard; some implementation details (e.g., EHF computation in Appendix C) could be clearer in the main text.

Limited failure case analysis: no discussion of scenarios where the method might not help, settings where SCOT might be preferable, or PDE properties that determine when spectral-spatial decomposition is most valuable.

Comprehensive and rigorously fair experimental evaluation following POSEIDON protocol exactly with identical training schedules, epoch budgets, and hardware; consistent improvements across 7 diverse PDE benchmarks (7-54% on Navier-Stokes, best results on all tasks in Table 1)

Principled architectural design with strong theoretical motivation: bandwise fusion with energy non-expansive property (Lemma A.3), Lipschitz bounds showing tighter cumulative bounds than Swin-style blocks (Prop. A.2), Sobolev-weighted defect bound (Theorem B.1)

Thorough ablation studies isolating contribution of each component (LFM, RG, FWL) with spectral analysis by frequency band (Figure 4) providing mechanistic insight into how components address different scales
Strong practical efficiency gains: 15% fewer parameters (17M vs 20M), higher throughput (158 vs 118 steps/s on FNS-KF), reduced memory usage, while maintaining or exceeding accuracy

Modular and reusable design allowing DRIFT blocks to replace windowed attention in existing multi-scale operator backbones; demonstrated long-horizon stability (T=100 on ApeBench) with sustained improvement and lower error-growth slopes

weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: only 2D flows evaluated despite discussion of applications to 3D and multi-physics; all evaluation on 128×128 grids; long-horizon evaluation limited to 2 ApeBench variants while other benchmarks evaluated at single final time T=1
